etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ryng, from Old English hring (“ring, circle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krengʰ-, extended nasalized form of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). Doublet of rank and rink.

definitions.definition: A circumscribing object, (roughly) circular and hollow, looking like an annual ring, earring, finger ring etc.
(jewelry) A round piece of (precious) metal worn around the finger or through the ear, nose, etc.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: The dearest ring in Venice will I give you.

definitions.definition: (UK) A bird band, a round piece of metal put around a bird's leg used for identification and studies of migration.
(UK) A burner on a kitchen stove.
In a jack plug, the connector between the tip and the sleeve.

(historical) An instrument, formerly used for taking the sun's altitude, consisting of a brass ring suspended by a swivel, with a hole at one side through which a solar ray entering indicated the altitude on the graduated inner surface opposite.
(botany) A flexible band partly or wholly encircling the spore cases of ferns.
(physical) A solid object in the shape of a circle.
A circular group of people or objects.

quote.citation: a. 1645, John Milton, “Il Penseroso”, in Poems of Mr. John Milton, […], London:  […]  Ruth Raworth for Humphrey Mosely, […], published 1646, →OCLC, page 39:
quote.text: And hears the Muſes in a ring, / Ay round about Joves Altar ſing.

quote.citation: 1944, Miles Burton, chapter 5, in The Three Corpse Trick:
quote.text: The hovel stood in the centre of what had once been a vegetable garden, but was now a patch of rank weeds. Surrounding this, almost like a zareba, was an irregular ring of gorse and brambles, an unclaimed vestige of the original common.

definitions.definition: (astronomy) A formation of various pieces of material orbiting around a planet or young star.
(British) A large circular prehistoric stone construction such as Stonehenge.
(physical) A group of objects arranged in a circle.
A piece of food in the shape of a ring.
(Internet) Short for webring.

quote.citation: 2002, Feroz Khan, Information Society in Global Age, page 100:
quote.text: Individuals looking to add their own homepage to a particular ring are, however, more or less at the mercy of the ringmaster, who often maintains a ring homepage listing its acceptance (or membership) policies and an index of its member sites.

definitions.definition: The open space in front of a racecourse stand, used for betting purposes.
A place where some sports or exhibitions take place; notably a circular or comparable arena, such as a boxing ring or a circus ring; hence the field of a political contest.

quote.citation: 1707, Edmund Smith, Phaedra and Hippolitus:
quote.text: Place me, O, place me in the dusty ring, / Where youthful charioteers contend for glory.

definitions.definition: An exclusive group of people, usually involving some unethical or illegal practices.

quote.citation: 1877, Edward Augustus Freeman, The History of the Norman Conquest of England:
quote.text: the ruling ring at Constantinople

quote.citation: 1928, Upton Sinclair, Boston:
quote.text: It's a blackmail ring, and the district attorneys get a share of the loot.

quote.citation: 2018 July 31, Julia Carrie Wong, “What is QAnon? Explaining the bizarre rightwing conspiracy theory”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: In a thread called “Calm Before the Storm”, and in subsequent posts, Q established his legend as a government insider with top security clearance who knew the truth about a secret struggle for power involving Donald Trump, the “deep state”, Robert Mueller, the Clintons, pedophile rings, and other stuff.

definitions.definition: (chemistry) A group of atoms linked by bonds to form a closed chain in a molecule.
(geometry) A planar geometrical figure included between two concentric circles.
(typography) A diacritical mark in the shape of a hollow circle placed above or under the letter; a kroužek.
(historical) An old English measure of corn equal to the coomb or half a quarter.

quote.citation: 1866, James Edwin Thorold Rogers, A History of Agriculture and Prices in England, volume 1, page 168:
quote.text: The ring is common in the Huntingdonshire accounts of Ramsey Abbey. It was equal to half a quarter, i.e., is identical with the coomb of the eastern counties

definitions.definition: (computing theory) A hierarchical level of privilege in a computer system, usually at hardware level, used to protect data and functionality (also protection ring).

quote.citation: 2007, Steve Anson, Steve Bunting, Mastering Windows Network Forensics and Investigation, page 70:
quote.text: Kernel Mode processes run in ring 0, and User Mode processes run in ring 3.

definitions.definition: (firearms) Either of the pair of clamps used to hold a telescopic sight to a rifle.
(cartomancy) The twenty-fifth Lenormand card.

(networking) A network topology where connected devices form a circular data channel. All computers on the ring can see every message, and there are no collisions, and a single point of failure will occur if any part of the ring breaks.
(transitive) To enclose or surround.

quote.citation: 2022 January 12, Paul Bigland, “Fab Four: the nation's finest stations: Eastbourne”, in RAIL, number 948, page 27:
quote.text: Today, when stepping off the train, you're presented with a bright and airy concourse that's ringed with a variety of facilities.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figuratively) To make an incision around; to girdle; to cut away a circular tract of bark from a tree in order to kill it.

quote.citation: 1887, Harriet W. Daly, Digging, Squatting, and Pioneering Life in the Northern Territory of South Australia, page 50:
quote.text: The ironbark trees are "rung" at a certain height top and bottom, and the bark detached in one sheet; it is then wetted, and laid out flat on the ground, huge stones being placed to keep it from rolling up again.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To attach a ring to, especially for identification.

quote.citation: 1919, Popular Science, volume 95, number 4, page 31:
quote.text: Ringing a pig of ordinary size is easy, but special arrangements must be made for handling the big ones.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To surround or fit with a ring, or as if with a ring.

quote.citation: c. 1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life and Death of King Iohn”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iv]:
quote.text: Ring these fingers with thy household worms.

definitions.definition: (falconry) To rise in the air spirally.

quote.citation: 1877 May 30, Gerard Manley Hopkins, “The Windhover: To Christ Our Lord”, in Robert Bridges, editor, Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins: Now First Published […], London: Humphrey Milford, published 1918, →OCLC, stanza 1, page 29:
quote.text: […]  how he rung upon the rein of a wimpling wing / In his ecstacy!

definitions.definition: (transitive) To steal and change the identity of (cars) in order to resell them.

quote.citation: A. Woodley, Trio: 3 short stories
quote.text: Gabe said that as Derry had only caught part of the conversation, it's possible that they were discussing a film, it was bad enough that they'd unwittingly been brought into ringing cars, adding drugs into it was far more than either of them could ever be comfortable with.

quote.citation: 2019 (10 December), Ross McCarthy, Digbeth chop shop gang jailed over £2m stolen car racket (in Birmingham Live) [2]
quote.text: They used two bases in Digbeth to break down luxury motors, some of which were carjacked or stolen after keys were taken in house raids. The parts were then fitted to salvaged cars bought online.  […]  Jailing the quartet, a judge at Birmingham Crown Court said it was a "car ringing on a commercial and substantial scale".

definitions.definition: (Australia, transitive) To ride around (a group of animals, especially cattle) to keep them milling in one place; hence (intransitive), to work as a drover, to muster cattle.

quote.citation: 2002, Alex Miller, Journey to the Stone Country, Allen & Unwin, published 2003, page 289:
quote.text: ‘I was ringing for your dad out there at Haddon Hill the year you was born. It was a good year for calves.’

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ringen, from Old English hrinġan (“to ring”), from Proto-Germanic *hringijaną. Cognate with Dutch ringen, Swedish ringa. Of imitative origin.

definitions.definition: The resonant sound of a bell, or a sound resembling it.
(figuratively) A pleasant or correct sound.
(figuratively) A sound or appearance that is characteristic of something.
(colloquial) A telephone call.
Any loud sound; the sound of numerous voices; a sound continued, repeated, or reverberated.

quote.citation: 1622, Francis, Lord Verulam, Viscount St. Alban [i.e. Francis Bacon], The Historie of the Raigne of King Henry the Seventh, […], London:  […]  W[illiam] Stansby for Matthew Lownes, and William Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: the ring of acclamations fresh in his ears

definitions.definition: A chime, or set of bells harmonically tuned.

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI):
quote.text: as great and tunable a ring of bells as any in the world

definitions.definition: (intransitive) Of a bell, etc., to produce a resonant sound.
(transitive) To make (a bell, etc.) produce a resonant sound.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: The shard-borne beetle, with his drowsy hums, / Hath rung night's yawning peal.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To produce (a sound) by ringing.
(intransitive, figuratively) To produce the sound of a bell or a similar sound.
(intransitive, figuratively) Of something spoken or written, to appear to be, to seem, to sound.
(transitive, colloquial, British, Australia, New Zealand) To telephone (someone).
(intransitive) to resound, reverberate, echo.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XXIII, page 40:
quote.text: […]  And many an old philosophy⁠On Argive heights divinely sang,⁠And round us all the thicket rangTo many a flute of Arcady.

quote.citation: [1898], J[ohn] Meade Falkner, Moonfleet, London; Toronto, Ont.: Jonathan Cape, published 1934, →OCLC:
quote.text: So he spoke, and it seemed there was a little halting at first, as of men not liking to take Blackbeard's name in Blackbeard's place, or raise the Devil by mocking at him. But then some of the bolder shouted 'Blackbeard', and so the more timid chimed in, and in a minute there were a score of voices calling 'Blackbeard, Blackbeard', till the place rang again.

quote.citation: 1919, Boris Sidis, The Source and Aim of Human Progress:
quote.text: It is instructive for us to learn as well as to ponder on the fact that "the very men who looked down with delight, when the sand of the arena reddened with human blood, made the arena ring with applause when Terence in his famous line: ‘Homo sum, Nihil humani alienum puto’ proclaimed the brotherhood of man."

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To produce music with bells.

quote.citation: 1669, William Holder, Elements of Speech: An Essay of Inquiry into the Natural Production of Letters: […], London:  […]  T. N[ewcomb] for J[ohn] Martyn printer to the R[oyal] Society, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Four Bells admit Twenty-four changes in Ringing

definitions.definition: To ring up (enter into a cash register or till)

quote.citation: 1983, T.C. Knudsen, John Hempstead, A Man's Guide to Women:
quote.text: The checkout girl rang it into his total, and he paid the bill.

quote.citation: 1990, The New Zealand Law Reports - Volume 3, page 75:
quote.text: On presentation of the item at the checkout the original price sticker was concealed from the checkout assistant and a sticker of $38.88 exhibited on the item. The checkout operator rang on the lesser sum, a mistake known to Dronjak. He was subsequently charged with theft.

quote.citation: 2011, Tracy E Whipple, A Friend's Last Gift, page 88:
quote.text: . The new cashier rang something twice and had to call for the manager to fix the register.

definitions.definition: (dated) To repeat often, loudly, or earnestly.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From a shortening of German Zahlring (“number(s) ring”) (coined by German mathematician David Hilbert in 1892). Apparently first used in English in 1930, E. T. Bell, “Rings whose elements are ideals,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society.

definitions.definition: (algebra) An algebraic structure which consists of a set with two binary operations: an additive operation and a multiplicative operation, such that the set is an abelian group under the additive operation, a monoid under the multiplicative operation, and such that the multiplicative operation is distributive with respect to the additive operation.
(algebra) An algebraic structure as above, but only required to be a semigroup under the multiplicative operation, that is, there need not be a multiplicative identity element.

definitions.definition: (mathematical analysis, measure theory) A family of sets that is closed under finite unions and set-theoretic differences.[3]
(mathematics, order theory) A family of sets closed under finite union and finite intersection.
